newsitem.title: UK: Several arrested after N. Irish policeman killed.
newsitem.headline: Several arrested after N. Irish policeman killed.

text.p: Northern Ireland police arrested several people on Sunday after an off-duty police officer was beaten to death outside a bar, apparently by a Protestant mob.

Father of three Gregory Taylor, 45, was killed in the town of Ballymoney, County Antrim. Television reports said at least seven pro-British "Loyalists", angered by a recent ban on a Protestant march, set on him in the early hours of Sunday morning.
"A number of arrests have been made. Inquiries are ongoing," said a Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) spokesman, adding that Taylor "died from injuries received when he was violently assaulted".

Protestant hardliners have been infuriated over recent months at being prevented from holding marches in the County Antrim village of Dunloy because of objections by its mainly Roman Catholic Irish nationalist residents.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, who was appointed to the sensistive Northern Ireland post a month ago after Labour's landslide election victory, condemned the killing.
"Any death in circumstances like these must be utterly condemned and our thoughts at this minute are with the immediate family of the deceased," she said in a statement.

In west Belfast security forces found a bomb detonation wire and 500 kg (1,100 lb) of explosives as they investigated an IRA claim that it had abandoned a defused landmine in a van in west Belfast, police said.

An Irish Republican Army statement hinted that one of its units had aborted a planned attack on security forces on Saturday and left the landmine in a van in the Poleglass district, a staunch Irish nationalist area.
"Five hundred kilos of home-made explosives were packed into two bins in the rear of the van," an RUC spokeswoman said.
It was the IRA's first reported hostile action in the province for six weeks, during which Britain has resumed contacts broken off 16 months ago with their political wing.
Protestant politicians immediately called for the tentative contacts to be abandoned.
The car was set on fire overnight following the IRA's claim made in a coded telephone call to a local radio station.
Children told journalists they had played inside the suspiciously parked vehicle before the fire and that it contained two containers of white powder.
The IRA, which has frequently left bombs in nationalist zones to catch passing British patrols, said it dumped the bomb after defusing it because civilians were nearby.

Britain ended contacts with the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein in February 1996 when the guerrillas scrapped a 17-month ceasefire by setting off a huge bomb in the Docklands area of London's East End, killing two people.
After winning power on May 1, Prime Minister Tony Blair resumed talks between government officials and Sinn Fein.
But Blair made clear the talks could only take place if the IRA refrained from using violence. Two rounds of talks have been held in the past 10 days and another is due soon.
